chapters.title: Growing up in two countries
paragraphs: Benjamin Netanyahu, usually called Bibi, was born on 21 October 1949. He grew up in Jerusalem, though the official biographies do not quite agree: the Prime Minister’s Office lists Tel Aviv as his birthplace, and the Knesset’s English page says Jerusalem. His parents were Tzila Segal and Benzion Netanyahu, a historian. He had an older brother, Yonatan, and a younger one, Iddo.

The family spent stretches in the United States while Benzion taught and did research. Benjamin went to high school in suburban Philadelphia, then came back to Israel in 1967. His father was active in Revisionist Zionism, the nationalist wing of Zionist politics. Growing up around American English, and American politics, later made it easier for him to talk straight to a U.S. audience.

chapters.title: The army, MIT, and Entebbe
paragraphs: He served in Sayeret Matkal, a special forces unit in the Israel Defense Forces. In 1972 he took part in the rescue of passengers on the hijacked Sabena Flight 571. He left active duty that year, then came back as a reservist for the 1973 Yom Kippur War.

He finished an architecture degree in 1975 and a master’s in management at MIT in 1976. He kept studying political science for a while and worked at Boston Consulting Group. Back in Israel, he did marketing for a manufacturer in Jerusalem.

In July 1976 his brother Yonatan was killed commanding Israel’s hostage rescue at Entebbe Airport in Uganda. Benjamin set up the Jonathan Institute in his memory. The conferences it held on terrorism were how he started to become known among Israeli and American policymakers.

chapters.title: Washington, then Likud
paragraphs: In 1982 he became deputy chief of mission at Israel’s embassy in Washington. In 1984 he was Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations. Both jobs put him on English-language television, arguing Israel’s case. He entered the Knesset on the Likud list in 1988 and became deputy foreign minister. He was on the Israeli delegation to the 1991 Madrid Peace Conference.

He won the Likud leadership in 1993 and led the opposition to Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin. He attacked the Oslo process: mutual recognition between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization, and a framework for interim Palestinian self-government. An Israeli extremist assassinated Rabin in 1995. Shimon Peres became prime minister.

sources.label: UN timeline of the Israeli–Palestinian conflict

chapters.title: A thin win, and Oslo stalls
paragraphs: In May 1996 Netanyahu beat Peres by a narrow margin, in Israel’s first direct election for prime minister. He was 46, and the first person born after Israel’s founding to hold the job. His coalition put security first, and wanted any land transfers from earlier agreements tied to Palestinian security commitments.

He met PLO chairman Yasser Arafat. Out of those talks came the 1997 Hebron Protocol and the 1998 Wye River Memorandum: Israeli military pullbacks, Palestinian security commitments, and more negotiations. Netanyahu’s government stopped carrying out Wye in December 1998. Labor’s Ehud Barak beat him in the 1999 direct election.

sources.label: Knesset record of the 1996 and 1999 contests

chapters.title: Finance minister, then back
paragraphs: He spent some time in business, then came back under Ariel Sharon, first as foreign minister and, in 2003, as finance minister. He cut taxes, cut spending and welfare benefits, and pushed privatization and pension reform. In 2005 he quit, in protest at Sharon’s plan to pull Israeli settlers and permanent ground forces out of Gaza. Later that year he took the Likud leadership back.

He formed a new government in 2009. That June, at Bar-Ilan University, he said he would accept a demilitarized Palestinian state if Palestinians recognized Israel as a Jewish state and the security conditions were met. Borders, Jerusalem and settlements were left open.

sources.label: Prime Minister’s Office on his economic policies

chapters.title: The long stretch in office
paragraphs: He led one coalition after another. His governments fought Hamas in Gaza and backed expanding settlements in the occupied West Bank. At home, the Knesset passed the 2018 Nation-State Basic Law, which says national self-determination in Israel belongs to the Jewish people. Supporters called that a plain statement of the country’s character. Opponents said it lowered the status of Arab citizens.

Stopping Iran’s nuclear program sat at the center of his diplomacy. In 2015 he spoke to the U.S. Congress against the deal the Obama administration was negotiating. Under Donald Trump, the United States recognized Jerusalem as Israel’s capital, moved the embassy there, and left the Iran deal. In 2020 the U.S.-brokered Abraham Accords opened formal relations with the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain.

Israel held four elections between 2019 and 2021 because nobody could hold a coalition together. In 2020 Netanyahu went into a power-sharing government with Benny Gantz. It fell apart before they were due to rotate the premiership. In June 2021 a coalition led by Naftali Bennett replaced him.

chapters.title: The corruption case
paragraphs: The attorney general announced charges in November 2019. The trial opened in May 2020. In Case 1000, prosecutors say Netanyahu took valuable gifts from businessmen Arnon Milchan and James Packer, and used his office in ways that helped Milchan. Case 2000 is about talks with publisher Arnon Mozes: friendlier coverage for Netanyahu, and possible action against the rival paper Israel Hayom. Both cases charge fraud and breach of trust.

Case 4000 adds a bribery charge. Prosecutors say he pushed regulatory decisions that helped the telecom company Bezeq, in return for better treatment on the Walla news site. Netanyahu says he did nothing wrong. He started testifying in December 2024 and asked the president for a pardon in November 2025. The trial was still going in November 2026.

chapters.title: Back in office, and the fight over the courts
paragraphs: He was prime minister again on 29 December 2022. The coalition included ultra-Orthodox parties and far-right parties tied to Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir. It proposed big changes to how judges are appointed, and to the courts’ power to review what the government does. The protests went on for months.

People in favor said elected leaders needed more control over policy, and that unelected judges had too much of it. Protesters said the changes would weaken the checks on a parliamentary majority. In January 2024 the Supreme Court struck down an amendment that had limited review of government decisions under the reasonableness standard.

chapters.title: October 7, Gaza, and a wider war
paragraphs: On 7 October 2023, Hamas and other armed groups attacked southern Israel. About 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken. Netanyahu’s government went to war in Gaza, saying it meant to dismantle Hamas and bring the hostages home. The campaign killed tens of thousands of people, drove most of Gaza’s population from their homes, and wrecked civilian infrastructure. In Israel, hostage families pushed for a deal, and the calls grew for an inquiry into what had failed before the attack.

In November 2024 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former defense minister Yoav Gallant. The judges said there were reasonable grounds to believe the two bore responsibility for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity, including starvation as a method of warfare. That is the warrant stage, not a conviction. Netanyahu rejected the allegations. Israel says the court has no jurisdiction.

South Africa filed a separate case against Israel at the International Court of Justice, under the Genocide Convention. Israel rejected that allegation. In 2024 the court issued provisional orders, including steps on humanitarian aid. That case is about Israel’s duties as a state. The ICC warrants are about the alleged criminal responsibility of individuals.

A U.S.-backed ceasefire in October 2025 brought the release of the last hostages from 7 October who were still alive. By November 2026 the UN was still recording strikes, casualties, and severe humanitarian need. Israel had also fought Iran directly in June 2025. On 28 February 2026 Israel and the United States opened a new war against Iran, and Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed. Fighting with Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon continued.

chapters.title: Family, and the books
paragraphs: He has three children. Noa is from his first marriage, to Miriam Haran. His second marriage was to Fleur Cates. He married Sara Ben-Artzi in 1991, and they have two sons, Yair and Avner. He has written several books on terrorism and Israeli security, and in 2022 he published an autobiography, Bibi: My Story.

chapters.title: An election, and no majority
paragraphs: In the election on 27 October 2026, Likud won 27 of 120 seats. That made it the largest party, but Netanyahu’s bloc lost its majority. On 8 November, President Isaac Herzog gave the first chance to form a government to Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief who leads the Yashar party. As of 15 November 2026, Netanyahu was still caretaker prime minister, and the talks were still going.

events: Birth
Born on 21 October and raised partly in Jerusalem.
Enlists in the IDF
Joins Sayeret Matkal and serves as a soldier and officer.
MIT and Entebbe
Completes his management degree. His brother Yonatan dies leading a hostage rescue in Uganda.
United Nations ambassador
Begins four years as Israel’s UN ambassador after serving in Washington.
Enters the Knesset
Wins a seat on the Likud list and becomes deputy foreign minister.
Leads Likud
Becomes opposition leader as Rabin’s government pursues the Oslo process.
First premiership
Narrowly defeats Shimon Peres in Israel’s first direct election for prime minister.
Wye River Memorandum
Signs a U.S.-brokered agreement with Yasser Arafat following the 1997 Hebron Protocol.
Resigns over Gaza disengagement
Leaves Ariel Sharon’s cabinet and later regains the Likud leadership.
Returns as prime minister
Forms a government and outlines conditions for a demilitarized Palestinian state.
Addresses the U.S. Congress
Argues against the nuclear agreement being negotiated with Iran.
Abraham Accords
Israel normalizes relations with the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain. Netanyahu’s domestic corruption trial also opens this year.
Returns to office again
After losing power in 2021, forms a government with religious and far-right parties.
October 7 and the Gaza war
Hamas-led attacks kill about 1,200 people in Israel and take 251 hostages. Israel launches a major military campaign in Gaza.
ICC arrest warrant
International Criminal Court judges issue warrants for Netanyahu and former defense minister Yoav Gallant.
War with Iran and a deadlocked election
Israel and the United States launch a war against Iran in February. In October, Likud remains the largest party but Netanyahu’s bloc loses its majority.
